field_rule: Use low fine-grass habit, actual narrow spikelet-bearing panicle, and narrow leaves to suspect aparejo; distinguish it from nimblewill by a positively seen scaly UNDERGROUND rhizome and true inner membranous ligule, not by inference from turf texture.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 214
habit.reference: Flora confirms low rhizomatous perennial, narrow interrupted panicles 1–4 cm and barely pointed lemmas; existing head/habit states supported.

diagnostic_checks.look: Expose a true underground SCALY rhizome
diagnostic_checks.check: Aparejo forms low patches connected by elongated scaly UNDERGROUND stems; true blades threadlike, usually 0.4–0.6(1) mm, involute. The eciliate short inner membrane is only ~0.5 mm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Nimblewill spreads via surface stolons and roots at lower aboveground nodes; do not mistake a white subterranean root for a scaly rhizome.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; existing photo roles need connected shoot-to-rhizome proof

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the very short interrupted head
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes a linear, INTERRUPTED contracted panicle only ~1–4 cm long on slender 20–40 cm culms. Branches are close, often appearing like separated spikelets on a tiny vertical spike.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Nimblewill panicles generally 5–15 cm and can be both terminal and axillary, with a weak mat habit.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; mature attached panicle photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the full glume and awnless lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: Single-floret spikelets about 1.6–2 mm; BOTH one-veined glumes generally 0.6–1(1.3) mm, whereas the three-veined lemma is about 1.6–2 mm and MUTICOUS (without a long awn). Compare several whole spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Nimblewill lower glume is minute/absent and fertile lemma commonly has an obvious 1.5–5 mm awn under magnification.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew; local scaled specimen and palea not checked

diagnostic_review.note: Referenced morphological descriptions checked. Whole-plant specimen, exact diagnostic organ photos, license eligibility and county native range not yet verified.

field_rule:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1288) — Use a hand lens to find two tiny teeth at the lemma tip. The Flora describes a short awn, 0.5–2 mm long, arising between them.

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas 1999, monocots excerpt p.212
head.reference: Hybrid panicle branches slender, erect-spreading. Existing open/airy key state retained. Hybrid determination from photo alone unsupported.

ligule.source: Same flora p.210: generic Muhlenbergia diagnosis
ligule.reference: Genus described with membranous ligule. Hybrid-specific structure still needs microscope check.

awns.reference: Lemma tip two tiny teeth with 0.5–2 mm awn between them; not a conspicuously long awn. Awn is not absent.

hybrid.reference: Hybrid formula M. lindheimeri × M. reverchonii, Central Texas. Morphology overlaps parents. Existing UT PlantPics-labelled external photos are unhosted due rights/rehosting uncertainty; zero key photo refs remain.

diagnostic_checks.look: Keep the parents and HYBRID name explicit
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew recognizes Canyon muhly (*Muhlenbergia ×involuta*) as a natural hybrid M. lindheimeri × M. reverchonii. Published intermediate-sized tuft, 60–140 cm flowering culms and often 3–12 mm membranous ligule are CANDIDATE clues, never proof of hybrid ancestry.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Lindheimer and seep muhly themselves overlap in ligule length and flowerhead stage; use authenticated voucher and expert diagnosis for hybrid name.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Accepted hybrid and parent formula verified; actual local plant hybrid specimen remains unauthenticated

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the intermediate upright open head
diagnostic_checks.check: Typical panicle open-elliptic, about 18–40 cm long and 2–5(7) cm wide, with ascending slender branches. The head shape is a useful comparison but not proof of intermediate ancestry from a photo.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Seep muhly usually spreads wider; Lindheimer often narrower, but Texas Lindheimer aging heads can spread too.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase; visual field state retained only as preliminary hybrid candidate

diagnostic_checks.look: Separate one tiny 2-toothed LEMMA apex and awn
diagnostic_checks.check: Published spikelet ~3–4 mm, one floret; glumes ~2–2.5(3) mm, equal, one-veined, persistent; three-veined lemma 2–2.5 mm with TWO small terminal teeth and a central awn 0.5–2 mm. Photograph attached floret with 10–20x and mm ruler before confirming.
diagnostic_checks.compare: One-awn florets also occur in parents. Tiny awn lengths overlap: hybrid status needs full specimen context and accepted morphology, not one tooth view.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew morphological account and accepted hybrid; key has ZERO hosted Canyon hybrid photos pending exact UT PlantPics image permissions

diagnostic_review.note: Referenced morphological descriptions checked. Whole-plant specimen, exact diagnostic organ photos, license eligibility and county native range not yet verified.

field_rule: Look down at the shoot tips: pale pointed leaf clusters surround a compact 1–2 cm head of about 1–5 spikelets. The flowering packets sit WITHIN the leafy fascicle, not at the end of a long naked flowering stalk. The true Munroa panels show verified same-taxon habit and flowering, including a locally archived Texas herbarium voucher; none alone proves all minute organs.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending
broad_group: Spikes, awns, dropseeds and remaining grasses

head.reference: 1–5 spikelets enclosed within short leafy fascicles; panicle only 1–2 cm, not borne as a tall loose head.

habit.reference: Small tufting perennial with short stolons bearing alternating elongated and clustered internodes.

ligule.source: Kew GrassBase under Erioneuron pulchellum versus FNA under Dasyochloa pulchella
ligule.reference: GrassBase ~0.5 mm hair-fringe true ligule; FNA 3–5 mm. Measurements conflict, potentially source scope or tissue definition; no absolute cutoff until same-voucher resolution.

awns.reference: Lemma awn 1.5–2.5 mm; no conspicuous long awn in usual field view, but not awnless.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look INSIDE short pointed LEAFY FASCICLES for the flowering packet
diagnostic_checks.check: Munroa pulchella (older Dasyochloa / Erioneuron pulchellum) is a dwarf perennial with alternating long and bunched internodes in its short stolons. Panicles only ~1–2(2.5) cm can hold **1–5 spikelets**, enclosed by expanded leafy fascicles, not on an obvious long naked flower stalk.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hairy woollygrass bears a compact hairy club above the lower leaves on a comparatively bare 10–30 cm culm.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Kew GrassBase under Erioneuron pulchellum and FNA under older name; actual leaflet-spikelet placement photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Dissect a 7–13 mm woolly MULTIFLORET spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew describes 6–12 fertile florets per 7–13 mm spikelet; persistent nearly equal glumes ~6–8 mm both one-veined. Fertile lemma ~3–5 mm and THREE-veined with TWO deep lobes and ONE short (1.5–2.5 mm) central awn. A frayed tuft isn't a new species.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Erioneuron pilosum often has 7–18 florets in ~12–19 mm spikelets and its lemma apex is less deeply lobed.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: GrassBase source; FNA ranges differ slightly and require same-plant scale; macro pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Keep LIGULE LENGTH disagreements explicit
diagnostic_checks.check: Kew GrassBase under synonym Erioneuron pulchellum describes a **~0.5 mm HAIR FRINGE** ligule, whereas the FNA treatment under Dasyochloa pulchella gives **3–5 mm ligules**. Do NOT teach one absolute dimension until taxon concept and tissue were independently checked in a Hays or Texas herbarium voucher.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Erioneuron pilosum also has an approximately 0.5 mm hair ligule; the hidden leafy fascicle and deep-2-lobed lemmas matter more.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Kew published quantitative disagreement; flagged for later taxon reconciliation and actual collar macro

diagnostic_review.note: Published botanical comparisons only; existing photos not individually anatomy/sex certified and source permissions not independently cleared.

field_rule:
Flora field cue (Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, p. 1296) — Look for a very open flowering head that is large relative to the plant. On the sheath, use a lens to see whether hairs rise from tiny raised bases.

Witchgrass is a warm-season fibrous-rooted ANNUAL, not a rhizomatous perennial. Published diffuse panicles ~13–50 cm, often breaking loose when ripe. Actual species panicle panel 3 and hairy-sheath panel 5 are useful, but neither proves a rooted annual or magnified tubercle-based hair origins. Never ID from a detached tumblehead alone.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

ligule.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 220
ligule.reference: Regional flora describes hair-fringe ligule; existing Hays card/FNA notes ciliate short membrane. Source interpretations conflict: preserve either observed state pending scaled inner-collar photograph.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look for the extremely open detachable TUMBLEHEAD
diagnostic_checks.check: Witchgrass is a warm-season ANNUAL with very diffuse, roughly 13–50 cm panicles and spreading branches. Its mature entire panicle may break off at its stalk and tumble. A detached head alone is not a species determination.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Purple lovegrass can also tumble as a mature panicle but is perennial, with tiny MANY-flowered spikelets rather than a Panicum two-floret spikelet.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Flora of North America; actual same rooted annual and attached late panicle required
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum capillare

diagnostic_checks.look: Examine the swollen hair bases on the SHEATH and tiny ligule
diagnostic_checks.check: The rounded leaf sheaths have conspicuous PAPILLOSE-BASED stiff hairs: each hair arises from a little raised bump. The true ligule is a very short MEMBRANE with cilia ~0.5–1.5 mm, sometimes appearing hair-only; either broad appearance is acceptable, not an assertion of separate organs.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hall's panicgrass can also have pustulate sheath hairs, but has a much more orderly ascending panicle and a perennial crown.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; photographic hair-base enlargement not certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum capillare

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure lower glume and two different mature florets
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives glabrous 1.9–4 mm two-floret spikelets; lower glume only ~1/3–1/2 their length with 1–3 veins, upper glume 7–9 veins; lower floret sterile, upper fertile floret smooth to darkening. Flowering units often persist after fertile florets shed.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Panicum coloratum has usually 2.5–3.5 mm spikelets with a male lower floret and developed palea; rooted life cycle and outer sheath hair matter.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Spikelet range overlaps other Panicum; no same-plant dissections verified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum capillare

diagnostic_review.note: Published Panicum flowerhead and floral/collar anatomy; fine-scale and winter same-specimen photo roles, local identity, and field acceptance pending.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O’Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, user-provided monocots excerpt, uploaded PDF p. 220
habit.reference: Flora confirms tufted perennial often knotty basal crown and fringed membranous ligule; optional short rhizomes supported by existing Hays Botany card, not proven by an undug photograph.

lower_floret.source: FNA Panicum coloratum and Kew GrassBase
lower_floret.reference: Lower floret staminate with developed palea (2–3 mm), paired with fertile hardened upper floret, versus lower sterile floret in many panicoid grasses.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect a SHORT knotty base, not a long crawling runner
diagnostic_checks.check: Kleingrass is a PERENNIAL usually forming an upright tuft with short knotty rhizomes or a swollen, scale-covered crown. It is introduced African forage grass; native plant recommendations must not be inferred from its presence in this key.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hall's panicgrass is a dry-soil native tuft, often with dry curling blades; switchgrass has more extensive, stout creeping rhizomes.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Kew supported; current Australian reference photo does not certify a Texas plant or variety
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum coloratum

diagnostic_checks.look: Compare the lower glume and fertile seed surface under magnification
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA reports ~2.5–3.5 mm paired-floret spikelets and a lower glume ~1–1.5 mm, about ONE-THIRD of spikelet length, 1–3-veined; upper glume and lower lemma about as long as spikelet. Fertile upper lemma 2–2.5 mm, smooth, shiny, lightly beaked.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hall's panicgrass often has a noticeably longer lower glume (~one-third to two-thirds) and ~2.2–3.9 mm spikelets in close clusters.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source-backed but many lengths overlap; not a solitary diagnostic test
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum coloratum

diagnostic_checks.look: Distinguish the developed STAMINATE lower floret
diagnostic_checks.check: In FNA and Kew GrassBase, the lower floret is male (staminate), with a well-developed 2–3 mm PALEA. The basal floret is therefore not just an empty lemma. True ligule is a short CILIATE MEMBRANE (~0.5–2 mm). Verify a flowering specimen, not an empty seed head.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Hall's panicgrass lower floret is generally recorded as sterile, but published palea accounts differ; both must be checked with same-stage florets before claiming a definitive separation.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Sex and palea only observable on appropriate flowering material; taxon/season variation flagged
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Panicum coloratum

diagnostic_review.note: Published Panicum flowerhead and floral/collar anatomy; fine-scale and winter same-specimen photo roles, local identity, and field acceptance pending.

field_rule: Dallisgrass usually 3–7 racemes with larger silky-margined spikelets, while vaseygrass commonly 10–20 racemes and smaller roughly 2–3 mm spikelets; counts overlap. Florida paspalum generally has fewer long branches and broad large oval spikelets. Bahia grass generally has two terminal racemes and lacks the distinct long marginal silky fringe characteristic of dallisgrass.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt pp.229–230
head.reference: Dallisgrass 2–8 one-sided racemes; long marginal hairs on spikelets and somewhat broad spikelets separate it from P. urvillei despite overlapping raceme counts.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the silky margin of a mature spikelet
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually 2–7 spreading racemes, each with PAIRED ovate pointed spikelets about 2.3–4 mm. The margins of the upper glume and lower sterile lemma have conspicuous long hairs.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Florida paspalum spikelets are more rounded and generally GLABROUS; Vaseygrass has smaller paired silky-margined spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; photograph with scale pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Count veins in the upper glume and lower sterile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA reports 5–7 veins in BOTH upper glume and lower sterile lemma; the lower glume is absent. View one removed spikelet under backlight, not a distant, hairy seedhead.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Vaseygrass has generally three veins on each; Florida paspalum has a 5-veined upper glume but only 3-veined lower sterile lemma.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; requires dissected same-plant pair

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the knotty perennial base
diagnostic_checks.check: Dallisgrass has short rhizomes less than about 1 cm, forming a hard knotty clump; ligule usually 1.5–3.8 mm and membranous. This does not mean it spreads with long surface runners.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Knotgrass has long spreading surface stolons; Vaseygrass also has a knotty base but tends to carry many more racemes.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; field habit alone not decisive

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.

field_rule: Florida paspalum tends to have big coarse basal clumps with relatively few long racemes and large often rounded spikelets. Dallisgrass generally has conspicuous long silky hairs fringing its large spikelets; vaseygrass often has much more numerous finer racemes with smaller spikelets. P. pubiflorum commonly has smaller 2.7–3.2 mm spikelets, and pubescence needs careful comparison.

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.230
head.reference: 2–5 long 4–13 cm one-sided racemes, larger glabrous spikelets 3.6–4.8 mm. Few branches overlap Dallisgrass; do not identify by number alone.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.230
habit.reference: Tall rhizomatous perennial with erect culms.

diagnostic_checks.look: Look for broad, nearly round spikelets without fringe hairs
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives 1–6 terminal racemes; attached paired spikelets about 2.9–4.1 mm long and 1.9–3.1 mm wide, often nearly orbicular and GLABROUS. Photograph against a millimeter scale.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass has conspicuous marginal silky hairs and more pointed spikelets; P. pubiflorum is usually narrower.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; mature attached spikelet needs macro QA

diagnostic_checks.look: Separate the upper glume from the sterile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: The upper glume is normally FIVE-veined, but the lower sterile lemma is THREE-veined, BOTH without the long marginal hairs seen in Dallisgrass. A single glume view cannot prove this two-bract combination.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass often shows 5–7 veins in BOTH; Vaseygrass three veins and silky margins.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; the two bracts must be compared on the same spikelet

diagnostic_checks.look: Confirm perennial rhizomes with the actual culm
diagnostic_checks.check: A robust perennial with rhizomes and erect culms often 80–210 cm; ligule roughly 1.2–3.3 mm. Use intact rootstock and mature panicle together, not the plant's height alone.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Vaseygrass can be equally tall but has 10–30 rather than 1–6 racemes in the typical FNA description.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA field characters; no county occurrence or specimen proof

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.

Florida paspalum usually carries larger rounder spikelets; dallisgrass has conspicuous silky marginal hairs on larger spikelets; thin paspalum's varieties can differ dramatically in foliage hairs and smaller spikelets. Without a true scale, don't force it.

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.232
head.reference: Usually 2–5(–7) racemes; spikelets in paired/partly aborted rows with variation in pubescence.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.232
habit.reference: Lower decumbent stems frequently root at nodes; never treat tuft as exclusively non-creeping.

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect paired spikelets for minute rather than silky hairs
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes paired elliptic or obovate spikelets about 2.8–3.6 mm. Upper glume and sterile lemma are usually THREE-veined and glabrous or have VERY SHORT hairs (under 0.1 mm), not long white fringes.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass and Vaseygrass can have obvious long silky margin hairs; Florida paspalum is usually wider and rounded.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA account; minute hairs need high-magnification photo

diagnostic_checks.look: Check the lower, creeping and rooting culms
diagnostic_checks.check: A perennial with lower stems usually decumbent and rooting at nodes, rather than a consistently tall upright tuft. Its flowering head commonly has 2–7 separated racemes about 2.2–7.9 cm.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Knotgrass is more extensively stoloniferous and typically has two near-digitate branches with mostly solitary spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; true rooting node image pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Confirm the glume is absent and compare branch wings
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes the lower glume as absent, paired overlapping spikelets, and an angular narrowly winged branch axis 1.1–2.3 mm wide. Note if immature ovaries make spikelets appear single.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Signalgrasses (Urochloa) have a developed short lower glume and an indurate, cross-rugose fertile lemma.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA genus anatomy with species-specific branch characters; dissection pending

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.

field_rule: P. setaceum often has one to few narrow racemes with relatively small spikelets and highly variable varieties differing in blade hairiness. Creeping wet-ground P. distichum typically has two terminal racemes and obvious stolons, while P. pubiflorum often has several racemes and larger spikelets. A single closeup of spikelets is not enough to prove variety.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.232
head.reference: 1–5 racemes, often long relative to plant; small spikelets and strong pubescence variation. Some prior rhizomatous coding requires further field confirmation.

diagnostic_checks.look: Find terminal AND hidden axillary flowering branches
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA reports 1–6 racemes per panicle; SHORTER panicles may also form within the axils of leaves and remain partly or wholly covered by their sheaths. Open a leaf base carefully.
diagnostic_checks.compare: P. distichum has mostly two terminal near-digitate branches and more extensive runners; pubiflorum has fewer axillary heads reported.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; field image of axillary flowerhead needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the small paired fertile spikelets
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually about 1.4–2.6 mm, elliptical to nearly circular and PAIRED. The LOWER glume is absent; upper glume and lower lemma are usually three-veined, with short or gland-tipped hairs possible.
diagnostic_checks.compare: P. pubiflorum normally 2.8–3.6 mm, P. floridanum is broader and up to ~4.1 mm; size ranges may approach one another.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; glandular hairs vary among varieties

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the tiny membrane and short rhizomatous crown
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives a membranous ligule just 0.2–0.5 mm and allows a tufted OR shortly rhizomatous perennial base, sometimes sprawling. A thick hair fringe behind the membrane can obscure its base.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Urochloa signals have a much more obviously hairlike ciliate collar and DEVELOPED lower glume; species identity still requires spikelets.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA account; the nine named North American varieties prevent rigid hair/size rules

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt pp.229,232
head.reference: Vaseygrass produces approximately 7–36 erect one-sided racemes, often conspicuously more than Dallisgrass's 2–8; counts overlap at 7–8 so secondary spikelet measurements needed.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count racemes along the main flowering axis
diagnostic_checks.check: Usually (4)10–30 separate racemes spread along a long upright panicle; most spikelets occur in PAIRS. Branch number is a useful first clue but overlaps with Dallisgrass at the low end.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass more often 2–7 branches with generally larger marginally hairy spikelets; tall native Florida paspalum usually 1–6.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; photograph of complete axis pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure one paired spikelet and its 3-veined bracts
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA describes spikelets about 1.8–2.8 mm by 1.1–1.5 mm, paired, with long silky marginal hairs; both UPPER glume and lower sterile lemma are THREE-veined. Lower glume absent.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass 2.3–4 mm and generally 5–7-veined on both bracts; Florida paspalum has no long silky margin hairs.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; measured upper-glume/lower-lemma comparison pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Distinguish a knotty upright clump from a stolon mat
diagnostic_checks.check: Vaseygrass is a robust tufted perennial with a knotty base of very short rhizomes under 1 cm; a true membranous ligule around 1–4(7.7) mm. This is not a long creeping knotgrass runner.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Dallisgrass also has a knotty clump: combine raceme count, paired spikelet size and glume veins.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA source checked; rooted crown and collar photo pending

diagnostic_review.note: Published morphology and measured descriptions, NOT field-measured local specimens, verified exact-source photo roles, or BONAP county nativity.

field_rule: Species first; lineage second. Three Texas lineages may look alike. These teaching photographs do NOT establish Hays County lineage or justify control.
trait_provenance: Hays Botany Poaceae existing individual species lesson; provisional broad field-state coding; final GrassBase and North Central Texas flora comparison pending

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.235
head.reference: Phragmites has densely flowered 15–40 cm panicles and LONG-HAIRY rachilla joints, but glumes/lemmas largely glabrous; unlike Arundo's hairy lemmas.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.235
habit.reference: Rhizomatous tall reed; this species-level description does not distinguish native/introduced lineages.

lineage.source: Annual Review of Ecology, Evolution, and Systematics — Phragmites North American lineages
lineage.reference: Native americanus / introduced australis / Gulf Coast berlandieri may look similar. Do NOT mark local Texas stands invasive or prescribe removal from morphology alone; exact lineage is unverified until suitable voucher/genetic work.

diagnostic_checks.look: Find long SILKY HAIRS on the rachilla between florets
diagnostic_checks.check: Common reed has 3–10-flowered spikelets, with WHITE SILKY rachilla segments between florets commonly ~6–10 mm. The fertile lemma itself is generally GLABROUS and long-tapered; do not mislabel the silky rachilla as hairy lemma.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Giant reed has the opposite distribution: virtually naked rachilla internodes and long hairs low on the lemma body.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA and peer-reviewed source; diagnostic closeup of separated floret/rachilla not certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Phragmites australis

diagnostic_checks.look: Check upper/lower glumes and the entire reed colony
diagnostic_checks.check: FNA gives lower glume ~3–7 mm, upper ~5–10 mm, and single large 15–35 cm (often drooping) plume on a rhizomatous 1–4 m reed. Inner ligule is a minute ciliolate membrane ~1 mm; dried husks and detached leaves often distort the apparent plume.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Arundo commonly has subequal glumes ~8–11.5 mm, broader canes and an upright plume. Head direction, height and color are only first sorting clues.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-based, true same-plant glumes/rhizome and winter stages pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Phragmites australis

diagnostic_checks.look: STOP at species level unless the lineage is established
diagnostic_checks.check: North American Phragmites includes native subsp. americanus, introduced subsp. australis, and Gulf Coast var. berlandieri; stem color, sheaths, ligule height and glume length help but can overlap. Field pictures DO NOT establish genetic lineage or native/invasive management eligibility. Record Phragmites australis lineage unknown if uncertain.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Do not label a photographed stand invasive or authorize control from the species name alone. Genetic test or expert vouchers may be required for lineage certainty.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Current review notes genetically and morphologically overlapping lineages; no Texas stand reidentification performed

diagnostic_review.note: Source-linked botanical comparisons complete for first checklist pass only; photo parts, exact lineage where relevant and Hays field specimens not certified. Endangered Zizania strictly observe without disturbance.

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.238
head.reference: Tightly contracted bristly-woolly panicle of numerous small spikelets; not a true simple spike.

awns.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.238
awns.reference: Conspicuous awns arise from GLUMES, not lemmas: avoid globally defining all grass awns as lemma extensions.

awn_origin.source: Flora of New Zealand, Polypogon monspeliensis; FNA/Burke
awn_origin.reference: The distinctive visible beard comes chiefly from long GLUME awns arising from emarginate tips; lemma may still be short-awned, so do not say lemma always awnless.

diagnostic_checks.look: Locate the real origin of the BEARD: AWNED GLUMES
diagnostic_checks.check: Annual beardgrass forms a very dense ~2–15 cm woolly-looking head. Each ONE-fertile-floret spikelet has TWO glumes with minutely NOTCHED tips bearing long (~4–10 mm) terminal awns from the notch. The prominent beard is mainly GLUME awns, not separate foxtail bristles.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria foxtail bristles are sterile branchlets BELOW spikelets; Hordeum glumes are awned too but bear three-spikelet node triplets on a simple axis.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: Burke Herbarium/FNA and Flora NZ; mature detached glume apex closeup pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of New Zealand — Polypogon monspeliensis

diagnostic_checks.look: Measure the much shorter transparent fertile LEMMA
diagnostic_checks.check: The fertile lemma is typically about HALF as long as the awned glumes (body around 1–1.5 mm); it may be awnless OR bear a delicate short additional 0.8–1.8 mm awn. Don't teach that all Polypogon lemmas lack awns, only that the obvious beard primarily comes from GLUMES.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Canarygrass has much larger winged unawned glumes and two minute sterile lemmas under one fertile lemma.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA / Flora NZ acknowledge some lemma awn variation; scale and actual glume/lemma separation needed

diagnostic_checks.look: Open the tall ligule and check the wet-ground ANNUAL base
diagnostic_checks.check: A soft cool-season annual common in wet disturbed ground, often geniculate at the base and sometimes rooting at low nodes. The LIGULE is a conspicuous lacerate/ciliate MEMBRANE usually around 3–10 mm (some international treatments allow wider variation).
diagnostic_checks.compare: Perennial reeds can also grow in damp ground but have very different many-flowered spikelets and much taller robust culms.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA/Burke region account, no same-plant rooted wet site photo/ligule certified

diagnostic_review.note: FNA/Kew/Texas botanical traits sourced; diagnostic photo crop, same-specimen measurement and county nativity require independent verification.

head.source: Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas p.242
head.reference: Annual cereal with compact awned true spike; usually two-flowered spikelets and narrow pointed glumes.

spikelet_units.source: Flora of North America Secale genus and Secale cereale
spikelet_units.reference: One 2(3)-flowered spikelet at a rachis node, as opposed to Hordeum node's three one-flowered spikelets or Elymus paired multi-floret spikelets.

diagnostic_checks.look: Count exactly ONE MULTIFLORET spikelet at each true rachis node
diagnostic_checks.check: Cereal rye is an annual/biennial with a two-ranked laterally compressed flowering SPIKE: one spikelet per rachis node, carrying usually 2, sometimes 3 florets. This is fundamentally different from barley's three one-floret spikelets at one node.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Little barley has three separate spikelets at each node, normally with the central fertile and two lateral reduced; Elymus generally has two multi-floret spikelets per node.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA genus / accepted species treatment; complete attached spike node photo pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Secale genus

diagnostic_checks.look: Separate narrow awned GLUMES from long lemma AWNS
diagnostic_checks.check: The glumes are narrow, stiff, keeled and roughly 8–20 mm overall but their own terminal awns are usually only about 1–3 mm. Fertile lemmas about 14–18 mm taper to much longer straight/scabrous awns around 7–50 mm. Glumes and lemmas are different bracts.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Polypogon has conspicuous LONG glume awns; rye's longest visible awns generally arise from the fertile lemmas.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA Secale cereale, mature glume and lemma photograph at matched scale pending
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Secale cereale

diagnostic_checks.look: Find the short membranous ligule and wheat-like ears
diagnostic_checks.check: A cultivated/escaped cool-season annual or biennial with mostly fibrous roots, narrow clasping auricles (~0.5–1 mm), and a small usually truncate/lacerate MEMBRANOUS ligule. Cultivated spike may not shed its rachis easily, whereas wild forms can fragment.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Canada/Virginia Elymus are generally perennial and bear PAIRS of spikelets at nodes; the head silhouette may overlap rye when immature.
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA species and genus accounts; variety/site-specific grown rye images not independently certified
diagnostic_checks.source: Flora of North America — Secale cereale

head.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.243
head.reference: Annual cultivated foxtail millet can have dense heavy purple/yellow or interrupted panicles up to 30 cm; bristles on many spikelets.

habit.source: Diggs, Lipscomb & O'Kennon (1999), Illustrated Flora of North Central Texas, uploaded monocots excerpt p.243
habit.reference: Annual with fibrous roots, not perennial rhizome.

diagnostic_checks.look: Find the annual crown and heavy spike-like panicle
diagnostic_checks.check: Foxtail millet is an annual without persistent knotty rhizomes. FNA describes a stout, dense 8–30 cm panicle, sometimes lobed below, with mostly 1–3 bristles around each spikelet.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Setaria parviflora is perennial, rhizomatous and usually has 4–12 bristles under each spikelet
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; mature head and actual annual base photo pending

diagnostic_checks.look: Inspect the seed-bearing fertile lemma
diagnostic_checks.check: The mature upper lemma tends to be very finely transversely wrinkled to smooth/shiny and about 3 mm long; the upper floret may break away separately. The bristles remain sterile branchlets and are not 'awns'.
diagnostic_checks.compare: Marsh bristlegrass generally has a more conspicuously transversely wrinkled fertile lemma
diagnostic_checks.certainty: FNA-backed; domestication creates much variation; macro pending
